title: Patrick's Confession
hookLine: Patrick calls himself a sinner, most rustic, and tells his story humbly
tomorrow: a prayer you put on like armor. what is it guarding?

cards: Every profile asks for the best version: three lines, best angle, wins only. How do you tell your own story without making yourself the hero? Patrick had a story built for bragging.
Taken by raiders, held captive, escaped, and later back in the very land that held him. Here's how he starts it: “Ego Patricius peccator rusticissimus.” I, Patrick, a sinner, most rustic.

teach.h: THE LEAST OF ALL THE FAITHFUL.
teach.b: He keeps lowering himself as he goes: the least of all the faithful, looked down on by many, his Latin rough, written by someone who never studied the way others did. So why write at all?
Because, he says, it would be wrong to keep quiet about the gifts God gave him in the land of his captivity.

teach.h: A STONE LIFTED FROM THE MUD.
teach.b: His best picture: before he was humbled, he was like a stone lying deep in the mud, and he that is mighty came and in his mercy lifted him up and set him on top of the wall. The order matters. First, I am a sinner.
Then, look what God did. Paul writes it the same way to Timothy: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” A neighbor tradition says something close.

teach.h: THE FOOL WHO KNOWS HIS FOOLISHNESS.
teach.b: The Buddhist Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: “The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.”
Both treat an honest look at your own lack as the place wisdom starts. The difference is real. Patrick's story turns on mercy: a mighty one reaches into the mud and lifts.
The Dhammapada's verse is about seeing clearly, and elsewhere it says you must make the effort yourself; the Buddhas only show the way. Shared: the honest start. Different: who does the lifting.

how: Christians in Ireland and elsewhere read Patrick's Confession as the saint's own account of his captivity, his calling and his thanks to God.

games.q: a classmate's college essay is all wins, and the teacher calls it flat. what would Patrick's Confession suggest?
o: add more wins, so the list looks even stronger.
name what you couldn't do, then who or what lifted you.
make it all about failure; hard-luck stories always land.
games.why: Patrick starts with what he lacked, then gives the credit to the one who lifted him. honest start, then thanks.

practice: If there's paper near you, write three short lines about one part of your story you usually tell as a win. First, what you couldn't do. Then, who or what lifted you.
Then, plainly, where you are now. Read it back once, slowly, and notice who turns out to be the hero.
